records.text: On 2023-05-20, the user asked for a 500-word overview of general local context in Edmonton, Canada, that people working on any sustainability issue should know, including in-text references and a bibliography.

The assistant described Edmonton as the capital of Alberta, Canada, a rapidly growing urban center with a population of over one million, located along the North Saskatchewan River. The response characterized the city as having rich natural resources, a diverse economy, and a distinctive cultural heritage.

The assistant stated that Edmonton's river valley and ravine system covers over 7,400 hectares and provides parks, recreation areas, and wildlife habitats. Edmonton has a cold continental climate, with long cold winters and short warm summers, and faces risks from droughts, floods, and heatwaves that challenge urban planning and infrastructure.

The assistant described Edmonton's economy as diverse, with energy, manufacturing, construction, and services among its key industries. It said the city has historically been closely tied to oil and gas, while recent efforts have sought to diversify through innovation, technology, and renewable energy to support sustainability and reduce reliance on fossil fuels.

The assistant described Edmonton as multicultural, with residents from many ethnic, cultural, and language backgrounds. It stated that Edmonton has one of Canada's largest Indigenous populations and a long history of welcoming immigrants, while noting social inclusion, equity, and access to resources and services as challenges.

The assistant stated that Edmonton uses a mayor-council form of municipal government, with a mayor and 12 city councillors elected every four years. The City of Edmonton provides services including water and waste management, transportation, and land-use planning, and has a role in addressing sustainability challenges and aligning local policies with the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

The assistant identified the City Plan, described as a 30-year vision for Edmonton's growth and development, and the Community Energy Transition Strategy, aimed at reducing greenhouse-gas emissions and increasing renewable energy's share of the city's energy mix. It also mentioned municipal programs concerning waste reduction, transportation, land-use planning, and ecosystem management.

The assistant identified greenhouse-gas emissions, urban sprawl, transportation, and affordable housing as ongoing sustainability challenges in Edmonton. It asserted that Edmonton's emissions are among the highest in Canada, attributing this in part to the city's historical reliance on fossil fuels.

The assistant's bibliography began with Statistics Canada's 2021 Census, “Population and Dwelling Count Highlight Tables, 2021 Census,” linking to https://www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/2021/dp-pd/hlt-fst/pd-pl/Table.cfm?Lang=Eng&T=301&SR=1&S=. The case study “Airbnb in 2020” says Airbnb began in 2008, when Brian Chesky and a friend rented their apartment to convention guests using air mattresses, calling the service “Air Bed & Breakfast.” The experience inspired a peer-to-peer room-sharing business. Airbnb grew from operations in approximately 190 countries and more than 4 million listed properties in 2018, when it was valued at an estimated $31 billion, to more than 220 countries and 7 million locations by 2020. It planned an IPO during 2020.

The Airbnb in 2020 case describes the COVID-19 pandemic as an existential threat to Airbnb’s business. Worldwide shelter-in-place measures and travel restrictions sharply unsettled accommodation demand. Some Airbnb hosts relied on booking income to help pay mortgages, while others owned properties whose viability depended entirely on Airbnb bookings.

The Airbnb in 2020 case says the company’s sharing-economy model faced criticism from city officials and traditional accommodation businesses. Critics argued that Airbnb hosts could avoid regulations and taxes imposed on hotels, motels, and bed-and-breakfasts; some hosts also faced legal issues under city and state rules governing hotels and apartment leases.

In the U.S. accommodation market described in the Airbnb in 2020 case, hotels and motels served travelers with lodging and differing amenities. Motels generally offered smaller rooms with direct parking access and facilities such as laundry, often near highways; travelers might use them for overnight stops on road trips. Hotels competed across traveler segments with amenities such as spas and fine dining, and some used spectacular views as an attraction. Recreation accounted for 70% of U.S. hotel market segments in 2020, business for 18%, and other uses, including meetings, for 12%.

The Airbnb in 2020 case gives estimated 2020 industry costs as a percentage of revenue. For hotels and motels: wages 26%, purchases 18%, depreciation 9%, marketing 2%, rent and utilities 7%, and other costs 27%. For bed-and-breakfasts: wages 28%, purchases 12%, depreciation 5%, marketing 2%, rent and utilities 10%, and other costs 40%. The case states that wages, property, utilities, and purchases together accounted for 78% of industry costs.

The Airbnb in 2020 case characterizes bed-and-breakfasts as small establishments, often with owner-operators renting a couple of rooms in their own homes. Guests might choose them for a cozy, personalized, quiet atmosphere and rural locations where the setting or a historically significant property attracts tourists. Bed-and-breakfasts offered travelers a slower-paced experience and connection with hosts and the surrounding community.

According to the Airbnb in 2020 case, hotels, motels, and bed-and-breakfasts were subject to city, state, and federal rules concerning matters such as property conditions, food safety, disability access, and alcohol distribution. Operators paid licensing fees and were subject to state and federal taxation. Building physical sites made rapid expansion difficult for hotels and motels, especially internationally; large chains could expand by buying existing properties or through mergers and acquisitions. Marriott International Inc. acquired Starwood Hotels and Resorts Worldwide in 2016.

The Airbnb in 2020 case explains that sharing-economy platforms let people offer spare capacity without a company owning the underlying assets. Smartphone use and falling technology costs helped individuals list resources or services, such as a spare room or occasional taxi service. The platform facilitated transactions and charged a fee.

Airbnb’s business model, as described in the Airbnb in 2020 case, earned a percentage of what hosts received for room stays. This marketplace model avoided the substantial real-estate operating costs of conventional lodging businesses and instead had technology-company expenses. The case estimates Airbnb’s fee at 11% per room stay, says Airbnb first achieved profitability in 2016, and reports that Airbnb announced nearly $3 billion in revenue and more than $90 million in profit at its 2017 annual investors’ meeting.
